key_gap: Both sides produced the identical correct explanation — the fridge is a heat mover (refrigerant boils inside absorbing heat, the compressor squeezes it hot, the back coils condense it releasing heat to the room; the pump does work; insulation slows the leak) — and both named the same gap: 'the fridge makes cold' treats cold as a substance, and the child's 'where does the cold come from?' cuts the shallow story exactly at 'makes.' The gap is the instrument: the human used the child's question as the diagnostic scalpel on the user's own naive sentence in the first pass — 'cold isn't a thing to add, it's a leak to fight' — and owned the breakdown immediately; the AI reached the same mechanism by generating and rejecting alternatives first (A 'makes cold', B 'sucks the cold out', C heat-pump loop) inside its HOW stage, stated the insight later and more cautiously, and only then emitted the final explanation.
learning_signal: For explanation tasks, the diagnostic instrument is the naive sentence in the user's own words, and a bright child's 'why?' is the scalpel: (1) in WHAT, parse the on-table explanation for the sentence that cannot survive a 12-year-old's follow-up question — the break point IS the gap, and it must be named precisely (cold is the absence of heat; the fridge moves heat out, it does not manufacture cold); (2) repair against the correct mechanism, never the vocabulary: boiling absorbs heat (evaporation inside), compression heats the gas (the pump's work), condensation releases heat (back coils — that is why the back is warm), insulation only slows the leak back in; (3) re-explain and accept the child's three questions ('where does the cold come from?', 'why is the back warm?', 'why doesn't the cold leak back?') as the acceptance test — a clean re-explanation that answers them without error is the deliverable; (4) the validation event of the method is 'it explains simply, so I understand it,' and it should be spent on the naive sentence first, before generating any alternative explanations.
suggested_improvement: Add a 'naive-sentence scalpel' pre-pass to the WHAT stage for explanation/understanding tasks: (a) extract the user's own explanation and test each clause against a bright child's 'why?' — the clause that breaks names the gap before any modeling begins; (b) in HOW, generate the rejected naive alternatives AFTER the break point is identified (the B-style 'sucks the cold out' rejection is then instant), not before; (c) require the decision packet's conclusion to be a plain-language re-explanation with the acceptance questions (the child's three) listed as verification evidence.

key_gap: The pure style executed its signature move and it backfired: it wrote the simple story ('just add more retries — computers are fast, extra requests are nothing'), read it back through the child's question ('doesn't that make it MORE struggling?'), smoothed the objection over ('it's busy, not broken; a couple of extra tries is nothing'), and declared the explanation complete because it explained simply — validating clarity instead of truth. The answer is wrong in three verifiable ways the style has no step to catch: a retry is new work on a saturated system (load amplification, and a thundering herd when attempts arrive together), a checkout retry is non-idempotent (double-charge/double-settle), and the incident telemetry (latency spike, rising timeouts) says persistent pressure, not a transient blip. The AI performed the three-fact check (saturation, idempotency, transientness) in its WHY stage, rejected blanket retries, and delivered the simple-but-correct rule: retry only idempotent + transient failures, exponential backoff with jitter, cap 3, circuit breaker, retry LESS under saturation — with the honest one-line version: 'Trying again is also work — and some tries can't be undone.'
learning_signal: The Feynman failure mode is validating explanatory elegance instead of correctness: the method checks 'can I explain it simply?' and has no step that checks 'is the simplified explanation true against the actual system?' — so a confidently smooth wrong answer passes the gap-check. When the decision is live and precision is required: (1) treat 'it's simple' as a claim to verify, not a sign of understanding — test the simplified explanation against the operative constraints (here: saturation = amplification, non-idempotent = irreversible, rising timeouts = persistent, not transient); (2) the honest simple sentence is the deliverable ('trying again is also work, and some tries can't be undone'), not the smoothest sentence; (3) simplification is safe only where it preserves the constraint the decision hinges on — name which complexity is load-bearing before removing anything; (4) a good re-explanation must be checked against the evidence, not just the child's comprehension — the child's 'wouldn't that make it worse?' was right, and the correct move is to answer 'yes, it would — so here's the version that doesn't,' not to smooth it over.
suggested_improvement: Add a 'truth-over-elegance gate' at the WHY/DO boundary for live-decision and precision-required tasks: (a) after any simplified rule is selected, run a mandatory constraint check — enumerate the operative constraints (saturation, idempotency, evidence direction) and require every clause of the simple rule to survive them; a clause that is false under any constraint must be rewritten, not softened; (b) in WHY, add a 'naive-proposal stress test': take the user's own recommendation and model what happens to it under the worst condition it claims to handle (here: retries under saturation) before generating alternatives; (c) in the decision packet, require an explicit 'what the simple version erases' line — the load-bearing complexity must be stated in plain words so the simplification cannot silently corrupt the decision.
